raw_response:
Eh, where do I start... I've worked these 10 mu for 35 years now. My wife and me are still out there most days, our son works in town at a factory so he only comes back at harvest time. Let me think about this year the way I always do.

I'll split the land like I usually do — about 6 mu I keep for wheat-maize, and the other 4 mu or so is cotton. The cotton ground is the patch out west that's a little sandier, doesn't hold water so well, so it suits cotton better. The better ground I keep for wheat and maize because that's our food and that's where the money is steadier. My neighbor old Wang, he quit cotton two years ago, said it's too much work for what you get, but I still do a little because the price was alright last year and I know how to do it.

**Wheat** goes in around October 10-15, same as always. The ground's usually warm enough then and if you wait too long the seedlings don't tiller right before winter. I use the seed from the co-op — the variety they sell is Jimai or whatever they have, I don't remember the name, but it's what most folks around here use. I'll plant about 15 kg seed per mu, a bit thick because the weather's been funny lately.

For fertilizer on wheat, before plowing I put down one bag of compound — that 15-15-15 stuff — per mu. That's 50 kg. Then come spring, around jointing when it starts growing fast, I'll top-dress with urea, maybe half a bag per mu, 20-25 kg. If the wheat looks yellow I'll put a bit more; if it's green and thick I'll hold back. I don't weigh it exact, I just go by the look. That's how my father did it and that's how I do it.

Irrigation on wheat — I do the winter water in November before it freezes, then green-up water in early March, then one at jointing, and one more at grain-fill if the spring's dry. So 3 or 4 times. The pump costs money but wheat really needs that water, you can't skimp. Last year I skipped the grain-fill one because the price of electric was up and I lost maybe 50 kg/mu, won't do that again.

I spray herbicide once in the spring for the broadleaves, and if I see the aphids getting bad around heading time I'll do one insecticide. Harvest around June 8-12 with the combine — I hire old Liu's combine, he charges 50 yuan/mu and does our whole village.

**Maize** goes in right after wheat harvest, no time to waste. I use the no-till planter behind the combine, or sometimes just broadcast and rotovate — depends on who's available. Plant mid-June, maybe the 15th to 20th. I use Zhengdan or whatever hybrid seed the shop recommends, costs about 60 yuan per mu but you can't go back to old varieties, yield is just too different.

Fertilizer on maize I do less than wheat — about one bag of compound at planting, and if the maize looks weak at knee-high stage I'll side-dress some urea, maybe 15 kg. Maize is tough, it grows in the summer heat and the rain usually comes.

Irrigation on maize — depends on the weather. If July and August rain is good I might not water at all. If it's dry around tasseling I'll do one watering, that's the critical time. Last two years I watered once each. Pesticide — I'll do one for borer around tasseling.

Harvest end of September, usually Wang's combine.

**Cotton** is more fuss. Plant around April 20-25 after the soil warms up. I use the hybrid seed, it's expensive, 70-80 yuan per mu, but you have to. I cover with plastic film, that's what everyone does here, speeds up the seedling.

Cotton fertilizer I put one bag of compound at planting and then urea in two shots — once at squaring, once at flowering. Maybe 30 kg urea per mu across the two times. I don't know the exact nitrogen, I just know it's about what I've always done.

Irrigation — cotton doesn't want too much, just once at flowering usually. Pesticide is the big thing on cotton, maybe 4-5 sprays through the summer for bollworm and aphids. That's why old Wang quit, all that spraying. My wife and I do it with backpack sprayers.

Harvest starts in September and goes into October, picking multiple times by hand. My wife, me, and sometimes I pay a neighbor 100 yuan a day to help for a few days.

Money-wise, I've got to watch it. Whole year I'm planning to spend around 4,000 yuan on inputs. If the cotton price drops I might regret the cotton, but I've got wheat and maize to fall back on. That's how we do it — you don't put everything in one basket.
